metaTitle: Black Bed Bugs: Brown Bugs, Black Droppings
metaDescription: Bed bugs are reddish brown, not black. See why a fed one looks dark, what the black spots on a mattress are and which black bugs get mistaken for them.
h1: Black Bed Bugs: Are Bed Bugs Black, or Is It Something Else?
dek: Bed bugs are reddish brown, not black. Here is what color they are at each stage, why one that has fed looks darker, what the black dots on a mattress are, and which black insects get mistaken for them.
excerpt: Bed bugs are reddish brown, not black. Why a fed bug looks dark, what the black spots on a mattress are, and the small black bugs most often mistaken for them.

quickAnswer.lead: **No. A bed bug is not black: adults are reddish brown, and young ones that have not fed are a translucent whitish-yellow.** One that has just fed is bright red, then darkens over the next couple of days as it digests, according to [Virginia Tech's bed bug identification guide](https://www.vdacs.virginia.gov/pdf/bb-identify1.pdf); that darkening is a likely reason one gets called black. The droppings and a handful of other insects really are black.
bullets: Adult bed bugs are about 3/16 to 1/4 inch long across the sources cited here, which describe them as reddish brown, rusty red or mahogany; none calls a live one black.
A bed bug that fed within the last couple of hours is bright red and swollen, then darkens and flattens over the next couple of days.
Hungry nymphs are almost completely pale white or yellowish and measure 1/20 to 1/5 inch.
The black dots on a mattress are digested blood, often in groups of 10 or more, and the EPA says they may bleed into fabric the way a marker would.
The black carpet beetle is shiny black and 1/8 to 3/16 inch long, close to the length of an adult bed bug, but it is a beetle that can fly.
Bed bugs walk; they do not jump, fly or hop, so a black bug that does any of those is something else.

body.text: Are bed bugs black?

No. Adult bed bugs are brown to reddish brown, and the young are far paler. [Virginia Tech entomologist Dini Miller's identification guide](https://www.vdacs.virginia.gov/pdf/bb-identify1.pdf) calls adults reddish brown and immature bed bugs a translucent whitish-yellow. The [University of California's bed bug guide](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/bed-bugs/) describes adults as rusty red or mahogany, and a [Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station identification poster](https://portal.ct.gov/-/media/caes/documents/bed_bugs/bedbugsandlookalikes11x17pdf.pdf) calls them tan to brown, looking more red after a recent meal. Mahogany is as dark as any of these descriptions gets. None of them describes a live bed bug as black.

That leaves three explanations for a black bug or a black speck in a bed: a bed bug that has darkened while digesting a meal, bed bug droppings, or a different insect altogether. For the size and shape of every stage, see [what bed bugs look like up close](/blog/what-do-bed-bugs-look-like), and for biology, bites and treatment start from [the complete bed bug reference](/learn/bed-bugs).

body.text: What color are bed bugs at each life stage?

They start white, stay pale through five nymph stages and end up reddish brown as adults, with a swing to red and then to a darker shade after every blood meal. Virginia Tech notes that a nymph has to take a blood meal before each of its five molts, so color is tied to feeding from the first stage onward.

body.text: Two things in that table matter to anyone who thinks they saw a black bed bug. First, the youngest bed bugs are the opposite of black: Virginia Tech says first-stage nymphs are so small that they are hard to see at all unless they are moving or full of blood. Second, the only shift toward a darker color that these sources describe follows a blood meal and plays out over a couple of days. A separate page covers [how nymphs change from one stage to the next](/blog/baby-bed-bugs-nymphs), and another explains [what shed bed bug skins look like and what they say about an infestation](/blog/bed-bug-shells-casings-shed-skins-canada).
Why can a bed bug look black?

The likeliest explanation is a recent blood meal. Virginia Tech's guide says a bed bug that fed within the last couple of hours is bright red, then darkens and flattens again over the next couple of days as it digests the meal. The guide never says the insect itself turns black, but it does say bed bug droppings are black instead of red because the blood in them has already been digested. Bed bugs feed every 5 to 7 days when a host is present, by the guide's count, so on that schedule a bug found in an occupied bedroom would have eaten within about the past week.
Two other things push the impression toward black:

items: **A dark base color.** The University of California describes adults as rusty red or mahogany, and mahogany is a deep red-brown. On an insect about 1/5 inch long, a color that deep may be read as black at a glance, particularly in poor light.

**Black droppings around it.** Bed bugs gather in groups after feeding, and Virginia Tech lists what those clusters hold: live bugs of several stages, shed skins, eggs and many black fecal spots. Its guide shows clusters on an apartment ceiling that looked like mold or mildew at first glance.

body.text: What these sources do not describe is a glossy, jet-black bed bug, a black nymph, or a bed bug that stays black when it has not fed. If the insect in question is shiny black, hairy, or able to jump or fly, count that as evidence against bed bugs. The Connecticut poster states that bed bugs do not jump, fly or hop, only walk, and Virginia Tech notes that adults are wingless.
What are the black spots on a mattress?

Black dots grouped along mattress seams are what bed bug droppings look like, and the droppings are digested blood. Virginia Tech explains that blood contains a lot of water, so a bed bug concentrates its meal and excretes the excess as semi-liquid waste wherever it goes after feeding. [The EPA's guide to finding bed bugs](https://www.epa.gov/bedbugs/how-find-bed-bugs) describes the result as dark spots about the size of a printed bullet point that may bleed into fabric the way a marker would. Virginia Tech calls the spots black. The University of California allows a wider range: usually reddish brown or dark brown to black, sometimes yellowish, roughly round or sometimes streaked, and they can be very small.

The spots usually come in numbers. Virginia Tech says they are often seen in groups of 10 or more, although where an infestation is light and a bug was only passing through, there may be just one or two in a given place. When an infestation is small, the guide points to these places first:

items: Along the mattress seams and on the mattress tag.
On the wood frame of the box spring.
Along the tops of baseboards and the edge of the carpet.
At ceiling and wall junctions, behind pictures and at electrical outlets.
In curtain seams where the fabric gathers at the rod.

body.text: A step-by-step bedroom inspection that covers those places is laid out in [where bed bugs hide and how to inspect for them](/blog/where-do-bed-bugs-hide).

body.text: How do you tell bed bug spots from other dark marks?
Check the color, the texture and what is lying next to the mark, because not every dark speck on a bed came from a bed bug.

body.text: Virginia Tech's order of checks is worth copying. Look first for other bed bug evidence close by, such as shed skins or hatched eggs, and only then fall back on touch: bed bug spots feel smooth because they are dried liquid, while German cockroach droppings feel granular. Every sign a mattress can show, and what to do about a mattress that has them, is in [the guide to bed bugs on a mattress](/blog/bed-bugs-on-mattress). A related page compares [bed bug droppings with the other stains they are confused with](/blog/bed-bug-stains-poop-droppings-canada).
Which small black bugs are mistaken for bed bugs?

Carpet beetles come first: the EPA says they can be easily mistaken for bed bugs, and the black carpet beetle is both black and close to a bed bug in length. The [University of California's carpet beetle guide](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/carpet-beetles/) describes the black carpet beetle as shiny black and dark brown with brownish legs and 1/8 to 3/16 inch long, and the top of that range matches the roughly 3/16 inch Virginia Tech gives for an adult bed bug that has not fed recently. Fleas, young cockroaches and bat bugs are the other small insects compared below.

body.title: The fastest rule-out
body.text: Bed bugs do not jump, fly or hop. A dark insect that does any of the three is not a bed bug, whatever its color.

Two rows in that table deserve a note. The cockroach description comes from [the University of Florida's German cockroach profile](https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN128), and a separate guide covers [what baby cockroaches look like](/blog/what-do-baby-cockroaches-look-like). Bat bugs are the one look-alike on this list that the sources separate only under magnification, which is why the checklist below ends with a second opinion.

Itching does not settle the question either. The Connecticut poster notes that the hairs of the varied carpet beetle can irritate skin, and Virginia Tech calls bites an unreliable indicator of bed bugs because reactions vary so much from person to person. Some specks are not insects at all: the same poster warns that seeds and lint can look remarkably like insects to the naked eye. Spider beetles, booklice and ticks are compared one by one in [the full guide to bugs that look like bed bugs](/blog/bugs-that-look-like-bed-bugs), which also explains how to have a specimen identified through a university extension office.

body.text: How do you confirm whether it is a bed bug?

Catch the insect, look at it under magnification and check the bed for the other signs; color alone will not tell you. For inspecting a mattress or furniture, the Connecticut poster's equipment list includes a bright flashlight, a hand lens, soft tweezers and a glass bottle to hold insects for identification.

items: **Capture it intact.** Pick the insect up with soft tweezers and put it in a small glass bottle or jar.
**Watch how it moves.** Bed bugs walk. An insect that jumps, hops or flies is not one.
**Check the build under a hand lens.** An adult bed bug is wingless, broadly oval and flat from top to bottom unless it has just fed.

**Match the color to a feeding state.** Bright red and swollen points to a meal within the last couple of hours, dark and partly flattened to a meal in the last couple of days, and flat and reddish brown to no recent meal.
**Search the bed for company.** Look along mattress seams, on the box spring frame and behind the headboard for black fecal spots, translucent shed skins and pearl-white eggs.
**Ask for a second opinion.** If it still looks like a bed bug under the lens, have an expert confirm it, because bat bugs can only be separated under magnification.

body.text: A bug that passes every check, with spots and shed skins nearby, should be treated as a bed bug whatever shade it is. The next step is [a complete plan for getting rid of bed bugs](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-bed-bugs). A shiny black beetle near a window, or an insect that jumps, calls for a different response, so settle the identification before treating anything.

faqs.question: Are baby bed bugs black?
faqs.answer: No. Young bed bugs, called nymphs, are the palest stage. Virginia Tech describes them as translucent whitish-yellow, and a hungry nymph as almost completely pale white or yellowish. After a blood meal a nymph turns brilliant red and looks like a plump raspberry seed. The University of California gives their size as 1/20 to 1/5 inch. A tiny insect that is dark all over is therefore more likely something else, such as a carpet beetle or a young German cockroach, which the University of Florida describes as dark brown to black.

faqs.question: Do bed bugs turn black when they die?
faqs.answer: The extension and agency sources behind this page do not describe a color change at death, so there is no well-sourced answer. What they do document is that a live bed bug darkens for a couple of days while it digests a blood meal, and that the skins nymphs shed are translucent to pale yellow, not black. Color is not a reliable way to judge whether a bed bug is dead or alive. Watch for movement, and check seams and bed frame joints for live bugs.

faqs.question: Are black spots on sheets always from bed bugs?
faqs.answer: No. Bed bug fecal spots are dark dots of digested blood, often in groups of 10 or more along seams, and the EPA says they may bleed into fabric the way a marker would. Rusty or reddish smears are different: they come from bed bugs that were crushed. German cockroach droppings can look similar to bed bug spots but feel granular, while bed bug spots feel smooth, according to Virginia Tech. Its advice is to look for other evidence nearby, such as shed skins or hatched eggs, before deciding what left the marks.

faqs.question: Is a black bed bug a different species?
faqs.answer: Nothing in the sources used for this page describes a black species of bed bug. The close relatives it can be confused with include bat bugs and swallow bugs. The University of California says they are told apart with a hand lens or microscope by comparing the hairs on the plate behind the head with the width of the eye: shorter than the eye on a bed bug, longer on a bat bug or swallow bug. A dark bed bug is more likely explained by a recent blood meal, since Virginia Tech says a fed bed bug darkens over the next couple of days as it digests.

faqs.question: What is the small black bug in my bed if it is not a bed bug?
faqs.answer: A shiny black beetle 1/8 to 3/16 inch long fits the University of California's description of the black carpet beetle, whose adults are attracted to sunlight and typically turn up near windows. A hairy, segmented grub with no distinct head fits a carpet beetle larva. An insect that is flattened from side to side and jumps points to a flea, according to the Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station. A dark brown to black juvenile with dark parallel bands behind the head matches a German cockroach nymph. If the specimen fits none of these, have it identified before treating anything.

faqs.question: Do bed bugs get darker as they grow?
faqs.answer: Yes, in the sense that adults are darker than nymphs. The University of California describes nymphs as looking like adults except for their smaller size, thinner outer skeleton and lighter yellowish-white color, while adults are rusty red or mahogany. Virginia Tech counts five nymph stages, each of which must feed on blood before it can molt to the next. On top of that difference between stages, every blood meal turns a bed bug bright red and then darker over the next couple of days.
